turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala asked Nikhil what grounds he had for accusing Sandip and his followers of oppressing his tenantry.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Bimala that he had witnesses who could attest to the oppression of his tenantry by Sandip's followers, and that he would not tolerate such behavior in his territory.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala asked Nikhil how his tenantry could be oppressed if they were free to come and go as they pleased from his estate.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip told Nikhil that he was wasting his breath, and that the Mussulmans were merely a trivial nuisance, a minor inconvenience that would soon be forgotten.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil warned Sandip that his flippant attitude would not deter him from taking action to protect his tenants and maintain order in the region.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was truly so naive as to think that a few empty threats from some local Mussulmans could possibly threaten the great Sandip's domain.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil warned Sandip that his carelessness was a sign of weakness, and that he would not hesitate to take action if his authority was not respected.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip told Nikhil that he was an alarmist, always predicting doom and gloom, while he, Sandip, was the one who truly understood the situation and knew how to handle it.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala asked Nikhil if he had any concrete evidence to support his claims of a potential threat from the local Mussulmans.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil insisted that the evidence was not a matter of conjecture, but of documented reports from the local villages, which he was prepared to share with Sandip.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was merely using these allegations as a means to further his own interests and undermine Sandip's authority

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil insisted that he was not motivated by personal interests, but by a sense of duty to protect the zamindari and its people.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip exclaimed that Nikhil was merely trying to distract him from the real issue, which was the zamindari's deteriorating crops and the peasants' growing discontent.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala turned to Sandip and asked if he truly believed that the zamindari's problems could be solved by simply ignoring the concerns of the local Mussulmans.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil warned Sandip that his dismissal of the threat was a grave mistake, one that could have disastrous consequences for the zamindari and its people.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip smirked and told Nikhil that he was beginning to think that his rival's dire predictions were nothing more than a desperate attempt to save face and salvage his own tarnished reputation.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala turned to Sandip and asked what specific actions he planned to take to address the concerns Nikhil had raised, and how he intended to balance the zamindari's interests with the needs of its people.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil warned Sandip that his refusal to take the threat seriously would only embolden the local Mussulmans, and urged him to take decisive action to protect the zamindari's interests.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had any proof of the supposed impending attacks, or if he was simply relying on hearsay and rumors.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Sandip that the zamindari's history was replete with examples of such attacks, and that he would not stand idly by while the people he was sworn to protect were put in harm's way.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Bimala where she would go, addressing her as the Queen.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he kept Browning among his books, reminding him of a contest they had over translating lines from Browning, and inquiring if Nikhil remembered it.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Nikhil and Bimala that he had managed to translate the lines into Bengali, but the result was unlikely to be well-received, and that he had once thought he was on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence had intervened to prevent it, and he recalled old Dakshina's poetry.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Bimala that it was pointless to search the bookshelves, as Nikhil no longer read poetry since his marriage, but that he, Sandip, was about to be afflicted with the 'fever fit of poesy' again.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil warned Sandip that he had come to give him a warning.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was warning him about the 'fever fit of poesy'.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that for some time, Mahomedan preachers had been stirring up the local Mussulmans, who were angry with Sandip and might attack him at any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had come to advise him to flee.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he had come to give him information, not advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Nikhil that if the estates were his, a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for him, and that Nikhil should intimidate the preachers instead of frightening him, and that Nikhil's weakness was also affecting his neighbouring zamindars.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he had not offered him advice, and that he wished Sandip would refrain from giving him his advice, as it was useless, and that there was another thing he wanted to tell Sandip, namely that Sandip and his followers had been secretly oppressing Nikhil's tenantry, and that he could no longer allow that, so he must ask Sandip to leave his territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was threatening him with fear of the Mussulmans, or if there was another fear he had to threaten him with.
